en: What it doesn't show: It doesn't mean the Peter principle applies to every real organization. How much competence carries over varies by role, and this model has no training, teamwork or motivation. In particular, it absolutely does not mean "promoting the worst performer" is good policy. In this simple model it only comes out that way because it keeps capable people at the bottom.

A simplified implementation of the ideas in Pluchino, Rapisarda, Garofalo (2010), "The Peter principle revisited: a computational study", Physica A 389(3). It points the same way as the paper (under the Peter hypothesis, promoting the best is the worst option) but does not reproduce its numbers exactly.

In the paper, "random" or "alternating best/worst" promotion did best, but in this implementation "promote the worst performer" scores highest. This appears to come from differences in details such as efficiency weights and how competence is redrawn, though this has not been confirmed.
Competence is a normal distribution (mean 7, SD 2) clipped to 0–10, and the efficiency weights from the top are 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. You can verify with node tools/validate-more.js peter.
The code is available on GitHub.
What Does Korea's Population Look Like in 2070? · Simulatio Lab
Change the fertility rate, migration and life expectancy and watch Korea's population pyramid evolve to 2070. A simple model, not an official forecast.
If the fertility rate stays around 0.7, what shape does Korea's population pyramid take over time? Change fertility, migration and life expectancy and watch it year by year from 2024 to 2070.
The population is tracked by single year of age, from 0 to 100+, and everyone ages one year each year. This is the basic "cohort-component method" of population projection.

Births: the total fertility rate (children per woman over a lifetime) is spread over an age pattern of fertility for women aged 15–49. Sexes are combined, and half of each age group is assumed to be female.
Deaths: mortality rises with age along a fixed curve, calibrated so each year matches that year's life expectancy. The slider sets how much life expectancy rises per decade.
Migration: each year a fixed number of people enter (positive) or leave (negative) at ages 20–39.
The 2024 age structure is an approximation, not official single-age data. It is scaled to published age-group shares (about 10.6% aged 0–14, 70.2% aged 15–64 and 19.2% aged 65+).

What it shows: If fertility stays at 0.72, this model gives a 2070 population of about 29.4 million with 54% aged 65+. Even raising fertility to 1.5 leaves about 38.6 million in 2070, below today, and holding the population near today's level takes large changes such as a fertility recovery together with migration. Aging comes not just from fertility but from the size of generations already born and from rising life expectancy.

What it doesn't show: This is not an official projection by Statistics Korea, nor a forecast. Because fertility is held fixed, sexes are combined and the 2024 age structure is approximate, its numbers differ from official projections. The model takes no position on which policy is right and does not evaluate the effects of migration or birth policies.

This is an approximation. It differs from official Statistics Korea projections. For reference, the median scenario of the 2022–2072 population projections (as reported in the press) gives about 36 million people and 47.7% aged 65+ in 2072, assuming fertility recovers from about 0.65 in 2025 to 1.08 in 2072. This model, with fertility fixed at 0.72, gives about 28.2 million and 54.6% in 2072, which is lower.

Figures checked (via press reports; I did not read the original Statistics Korea tables): 2023 total fertility rate 0.72 (0.78 in 2022); 2024 age shares 70.2% aged 15–64 and 19.2% aged 65+; total population about 51.7–52 million; 2023 life expectancy 83.5 (OECD Health Statistics).

Single-year population counts are not official values. The shape is built from approximate annual births and survival, and the three age-group totals are scaled to the published shares. So the 2024 median age comes out at about 47.5 in the model, which may differ from the actual value.

Births spread the fertility rate over an age curve for women aged 15–49 (mean 32.5, SD 4.5), and deaths use an exponentially rising mortality curve calibrated to life expectancy. You can verify with node tools/validate-population.js.
The reference lines in graph ② (fertility 0.7 and 1.5) and graph ④ keep your migration and life-expectancy settings and change only the fertility rate.
The code is available on GitHub.
What Happens When Queue-Jumping Spreads? · Simulatio Lab
Can order survive when queue-jumping pays? Change the strength of punishment and see when order holds.
Cutting in line pays off, and being cut costs you. If everyone cuts, the line falls apart. But what if some people scold cutters? The catch is that scolding has a cost too.
